note: Reading trails: ordered sequences of existing stories. The 'why' lines are editorial connectors, not claims; every fact stays in the stories, with its source.

trails.title: Myths first
trails.intro: Six ideas about Africa that sound solid and fall apart on contact with the record.

steps.why: Start with the biggest slip: treating a continent as one place.
Then the map itself, which shrinks the continent.
Next, a word that flattens millions of people into a box.
Then a phrase that hides a religion, a belief and a set of accusations.
Then a custom that reverses what many readers expect.
Finish with the language that does not exist.

trails.title: Kingdoms and other ways to rule
trails.intro: From the Nile to the Swahili coast and the Gold Coast: powers you were rarely taught, and one that had no king.

steps.why: Begin on the Nile, with a kingdom that ruled Egypt.
Move up to the highlands of the Red Sea trade.
Cross to West Africa and its gold.
Go down the East African coast to the other gold trade.
Back to West Africa, to a stool that stands for a nation.
End with a system of government without monarchs.

trails.title: Lines on the map
trails.intro: How borders, plans and labels were drawn for Africa, and what they left behind.

steps.why: Start with the conference everyone mentions.
Then check how complete the colonial map really was.
Look at a plan that treated the continent as Europe's extension.
See how colonial categories entered families.
Follow one case of children caught between those categories.
Finish with a name on the map, and what a name cannot tell.

trails.title: On the plate
trails.intro: Six foods, and the crops, trade and arguments behind them.

steps.why: Start with a crop that came from the Americas.
See how staples became the core of the meal.
Follow one dish across borders and arguments.
Go to the highlands, where bread is also the plate.
Stay there for the bean the world took away.
End in the Maghreb, with a dish four countries share.

trails.title: Ways of knowing and keeping order
trails.intro: Oral records, birds, masks and low roofs: how knowledge and accountability work without paper.

steps.why: Begin by testing the idea that history was only spoken.
Then a kind of knowledge shared between people and birds.
Then a belief about twins that shapes carving and care.
Then masks that let people criticise chiefs.
Then a meeting place built to keep tempers down.
End with a code of honour worn on the face.
